title: Function Vectors in Large Language Models
question: Do ICL tasks get represented by a compact vector that can trigger the task on new inputs?
mechanism: Causal mediation: mean task-conditioned activation of each attention head (abar = mean over ICL prompts, Eq. 2); score each head by CIE(a | p~) = f(p~ | a := abar)[y] - f(p~)[y] on uninformative (shuffled-label) prompts (Eq. 3); keep top heads. The function vector (FV) is the sum of selected head outputs at the last token; it is added to the residual stream at one layer of a zero-shot prompt (v_t FV, Eq. 5).
training: none (forward passes and activation patching over ICL prompts; no gradient training reported)
setup: GPT-J, GPT-NeoX, Llama 2 (70B); over 40 ICL tasks (abstract and intro)
numbers: GPT-J: baseline on uninformative input 39.1 +/- 1.2% and 5.5 +/- 0.8%; with v_t FV 90.8 +/- 0.9% and 57.5 +/- 1.7% (results table; column headers not captured in extracted text)
Llama 2 (70B): baseline on uninformative input 52.3 +/- 2.2% and 8.2 +/- 0.7%; with v_t FV 96.5 +/- 0.5% and 83.8 +/- 0.7% (same table)
limits: Authors report that FVs encode the output space of the function but that this information alone does not reconstruct an FV; composition by vector sum works only 'to some extent'. Head localization is task-specific, and the study is limited to the listed tasks and models.
evidence_quote: Using causal mediation analysis on a diverse range of in-context-learning (ICL) tasks, we find that a small number attention heads transport a compact representation of the demonstrated task, which we call a function vector (FV).

novelty_note.D: Converts in-context demonstrations (not a system prompt) into a single activation vector, the FV, that is injected into a zero-shot prompt to reproduce the task.

title: In-Context Learning Creates Task Vectors
question: Can ICL be understood as compressing demonstrations into a single query-independent task vector that parameterizes a function applied to the query?
mechanism: Split the forward pass into A (demonstrations -> theta) and f (query + theta -> output). theta is the hidden state at the '->' token at layer L, computed with a dummy query x' (e.g. Plum) so theta does not depend on the query. f is a forward pass on the query alone, with attention to the demonstrations blocked, into which theta is patched at layer L. L is chosen on a development set (accuracy peaks at an intermediate layer for all models).
training: none (forward passes only; no gradient training reported)
setup: LLaMA 7B/13B/30B, GPT-J 6B, Pythia 2.8B/6.9B/12B; 18 tasks in algorithmic, translation, linguistic and factual-knowledge categories; single-token outputs
numbers: Across all models, the separated A/f procedure keeps around 80-90% of regular ICL accuracy (Sec. 3 text; exact table not confirmed from extracted text)
limits: Authors list open questions on how the task vector is constructed and how it is used to compute the output. Experiments use single-token outputs only (stated simplification). Patching layer L is a free parameter selected on dev data.
evidence_quote: To make θ independent of the query x, we use a dummy query (x′ = Plum) and use the representation of → at the Lth layer as θ.

novelty_note.D: A task vector built from in-context demonstrations is patched into the residual stream of a later forward pass, so demonstrations become an activation intervention; the paper does not handle system prompts.

title: How Few-Shot Examples Add Up: A Causal Decomposition of Function Vectors in In-Context Learning
venue: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306 (2026), as stated in the paper header
question: How do individual few-shot examples combine into a function vector (FV), and what do attention contextualization and the QK/V pathways contribute?
mechanism: Per-example sub-FV v_i is the FV extracted with attention restricted so the final token sees only example i and the query. The full n-shot FV is fitted as v_FV ~ sum_i w_i v_i by ordinary least squares, with weights w_i shared across a batch of prompts. Injection accuracy Acc_max (max over layer and scale) is the quality score. An uncontextualized ablation removes cross-example attention. A causal decomposition splits the effect into QK-routing and V-update pathways.
training: none (OLS fit of global weights and forward-pass ablations; no model training reported)
setup: Discrete mapping toy tasks; model names and exact task count not recovered from extracted text (appendix not fully extracted)
numbers: Reconstruction fit, contextualized and uncontextualized settings: (mean cosine >= 0.925, mean R2 >= 0.875) (text near Sec. 4; column interleaving in extraction)
limits: Authors state that the study focuses on discrete mapping toy tasks and that long-horizon or compositional reasoning remains open. Value-pathway effects are heterogeneous and not fully characterized. Conclusions are bounded by the FV-head localization procedure.
evidence_quote: The FV extracted under this restricted attention graph is denoted vi

novelty_note.E: Predicts a multi-demonstration FV as a weighted linear sum of per-example sub-FVs before composition, a partial additivity model. It does not predict interference between separately applied patches, so this flag is weak.

title: Training-Free Task Vectors for LLM Behavioral Control
venue: NeurIPS 2026 (40th Conference), as stated in the paper header
question: Can steering vectors be turned into persistent, compositional weight-space edits without any fine-tuning?
mechanism: Steering vector s_l = mean residual difference between positive and negative contrastive prompt sets at layer l (Eq. 1); normalize s-bar = s/||s||_2. For a module W (d x l) with SVD W = sum_i sigma_i u_i v_i^T and expected input mu, TFTV(W, s-bar, mu) = s-bar (sum_i sign(mu^T v_i) sigma_i v_i)^T (Eq. 2), a rank-one matrix. Edit W <- W + alpha * TFTV on a chosen module set (Eq. 3). Property 1: ||TFTV||_F = ||W||_F, so the update matches the weight norm.
training: none (forward-pass statistics on contrastive prompts; completions are filtered by an LLM judge; no gradient training)
setup: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, gemma-4-E2B-it, Ministral-3-14B-Instruct; five traits (incl. evil, hallucination, sycophancy); MMLU and GSM8K for utility
numbers: Exceeds the strongest training-free baseline in trait score in five of six settings 'by 5.57-53.38 points' (Sec. 5.1, text)
Llama MMLU stays within 0.15 points of the base model across settings (Sec. 5.1 text; Table 2)
limits: Authors state that TFTVs do not eliminate the trade-off between trait control and utility, especially under stronger or composed edits. Performance depends on which modules and layers are edited, and automatic selection is left as future work. Misuse risk is noted because edits are persistent.
evidence_quote: TFTVs convert activation steering directions into rank-one weight updates using only forward-pass statistics

novelty_note.A: Builds a rank-one weight edit from a steering direction plus the SVD of the target matrix, with no training; the closed-form construction uses forward-pass means and the top singular vectors.

title: Steer Like the LLM: Activation Steering that Mimics Prompting
question: Can activation steering be made faithful to prompt steering by learning token-specific steering coefficients that imitate the prompt's effect?
mechanism: Prompt steering is written as an additive change to activations, Al|PS = Al + Delta_PS (Eq. 3). Prompt Steering Replacement (PSR) approximates it: Al|AS = Al + alpha * lambda(Al; theta) * z_attr,l (Eq. 7), where lambda(a; theta) = ReLU(a . w + b) is a per-token scalar coefficient on the layer's own activations (Eq. 8) and z_attr,l is a rank-1 direction. S-PSR edits one layer; A-PSR edits all layers sequentially. Parameters (w, b, z) are trained so the steered activations or output log-likelihood match those of prompt-steered runs, using triplets (x, x', y') filtered by judges.
training: yes: per attribute, gradient training of (w, b, z) on prompt-steered response triplets. Persona-Vectors set: 100 positive and 100 negative prompt pairs, 10 sampled responses per prompt; AxBench: 72 training concepts (Sec. 4 text)
setup: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (plus a third model not confirmed from extracted text); Persona Vectors (trait alignment at coherence 80); AxBench; IFEval
numbers: Text claim (Sec. 5, Persona Vectors): A-PSR (MSE) outperforms prompt steering for all three language models, A-ConstMSE for 2 of 3 (table cells not used because column headers are interleaved in the extraction)
limits: Rank-1 PSR is not expressive enough for all IFEval instruction types: for some types the MSE loss barely improves and prompting stays stronger. Log-likelihood training helped where MSE did not. The authors state the work is a first instantiation of the framework.
evidence_quote: the strength of prompt steering interventions varies significantly across token positions

novelty_note.B: The per-token steering coefficient is a learned ReLU probe on the layer's own hidden state (Eq. 8) that scales a steering vector. It is trained rather than a fixed rule, so it is close to B but not training-free.
novelty_note.D: Trains a replacement model so that an activation intervention reproduces the activation effect of a prompt-based steering instruction.

title: Prompt-Activation Duality: Improving Activation Steering via Attention-Level Interventions
question: Why does residual-stream persona steering lose coherence over multi-turn dialogue, and can steering enter through attention so it follows prompt-mediated pathways?
mechanism: GCAD. Extract the system-prompt contribution to attention: Delta^(l) = mean over positive prompts of the cropped attention-delta, sum over system-prompt source tokens of alpha_{t,i} V_i W_o (Eq. 7). Gate per token: c_i = 2 c_base * sigmoid(s * (d_i - dbar)), where d_i is the head-averaged pre-softmax query-key compatibility with mean system-prompt keys (Eqs. 9-10). Update: a_steered = a + c_t * Delta, applied at the attention output of layers 9-19 (c_base = 3.5, s = 1.5).
training: none (contrastive prompt sets are run forward; no gradient training reported)
inference_cost: one extra dot product per head for the gate, according to the paper (Sec. 4)
setup: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; multi-turn persona steering over 60 conversations; 15-trait average; trait and coherence scored 0-100
numbers: On the main multi-turn benchmark, GCAD improves average coherence drift from -18.6 to -1.9 and raises turn-10 trait expression from 78.0 to 93.1 (abstract)
limits: No limitations section was extracted. The paper reports that a trait with a peak at layer 9, outside the GCAD range, still degrades badly under baseline steering (Humorous). Evaluation is on persona traits with model-assigned scores.
evidence_quote: Since di reuses queries and keys already computed by the model, the gate adds only one dot product per head

novelty_note.B: The gate is a centered sigmoid of a query-key dot product computed from the model's own Q and K, with no separate classifier, and it scales the steering per token.
novelty_note.D: Extracts the steering signal from the system-prompt contribution to attention (cropped attention-delta) and re-injects it at the same attention site.

title: One Token Can Be Enough: Bridging Prompting and Activation Steering with Prefix Steering
question: Under what conditions can steering one token reproduce prompt-induced attention outputs, and does a brief intervention at the final prompt token keep control while preserving capability?
mechanism: Prefix Steering: apply an existing additive steering direction (or COAST operator) over a short span of tokens starting at the final prompt token, with no intervention after that span. Theory: under fixed-state attention assumptions, steering one existing token can match the attention-head output of an added prompt token exactly when W^K(h_p - h_tn) and W^K r lie in a matching subspace U, with error growing with distance from that set (Lemmas 1-2).
setup: Four models and five tasks; OLMo 3 7B for the duration sweep, HarmBench (control) and MMLU-Pro (capability); additive steering and COAST
limits: The authors state that the attention-level match does not determine the best steering strength, because repeated interventions also change later representations. The theory relies on fixed-state assumptions and does not establish equivalence with prompting. No numeric result table was extracted; the duration results are reported in Figure 3 (not read numerically).
evidence_quote: directions and operators over a short span starting at the final prompt token, with no further direct intervention afterward

title: PRISM: Recovering Instruction Sets from Language Model Activations
question: Can a frozen model's activations be decoded into the full set of instructions, constraints and subgoals that steer its response?
mechanism: Activation snapshot H_l = residual-stream activations at selected generated-token positions of a frozen target model (prompt positions excluded). A learned projection maps H_l into the embedding space as a soft prefix to an interpreter that reuses the base weights with LoRA and decodes a bullet list. Training: supervised pretraining, then GRPO where an LLM judge scores coverage and hallucinated bullets, reward R = coverage minus penalties, and the policy update uses group-relative advantages.
training: yes: supervised pretraining on instruction lists, then judge-guided GRPO (RL) on the interpreter; training data includes benign multi-instruction sets and 24,953 public prompt-injection examples (intro/Sec. 3 text)
setup: Target model Qwen3.5-9B (also Gemma and Ministral reporters); benign, constrained, prompt-injection and hidden-objective evaluation sets; judge calibrated with Cohen's kappa
numbers: PRISM (Qwen3.5-9B) reaches 0.754 reward and 0.767 coverage, with 0.020 hallucination (Table 1 average)
Average reward 0.754 vs 0.532 for the strongest non-PRISM baseline (intro)
limits: Authors state PRISM is a monitoring method, not a complete safety intervention. Evaluation depends on oracle-generated instruction lists and judge-based semantic scoring. Results are a controlled testbed, not long agent traces, and only the Qwen seeds have variance reported.
evidence_quote: A learned projection maps these states into the model’s embedding space, where they are consumed as a soft prefix by the interpreter

title: Memory Inception: Latent-Space KV Cache Manipulation for Steering LLMs
question: Can reminder or guidance text be held as latent KV slots that attend only at selected layers and heads, instead of being cached at every layer or added as a residual offset?
mechanism: A memory bank B = {(k_m, v_m)} of latent KV slots is encoded from the guidance text. At a selected site, the bank is concatenated with the prompt KV cache (Eq. 2). Sites are chosen by a calibration selector: score a_{l,u} = max_j q k_target / sqrt(d) - max_j q k_ref / sqrt(d) per unit, keep top-k units per layer and top-m layers, with layer gains rho_l. Multi-bank routing is a softmax over bank evidence, with size-normalized log-sum-exp scores (Eqs. 4-5).
training: none (training-free; calibration-time selector uses reference banks and task calibration examples)
inference_cost: KV-storage reduction only: 6.4x in the long-context Llama case and 60-118x in other settings (Table 1 and Sec. 5). Realized latency and VRAM were not measured.
setup: Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen3-30B-A3B; personality steering vs CAA and prompting; HARDMath and PHYSICS for structured reasoning
numbers: Qwen3 DAS: more than doubling CAA on Qwen3 (0.270 vs. 0.115) (results text after Table 1)
Outperforms visible prompting on HARDMath and PHYSICS in 10/12 subject x mode cells (abstract)
Content-matched KV storage cut by up to 118x (abstract; 60-118x in Table 1)
limits: Authors report: slots that are noisy, overspecific or too broad may fail in new settings; the selector needs task-specific calibration examples, so MI is not zero-design; results are partly backbone-dependent (Llama shows a sharper controllability-quality trade-off); cache analysis measures storage, not latency. Authors note the mechanism could be misused for covert behaviour shaping.
evidence_quote: At a selected site, MI conceptually augments the prompt cache with these slots:

novelty_note.D: Encodes a reminder or guidance text into latent KV slots that are attached at selected attention sites, so instruction-like text becomes an attention-level modification.
novelty_note.F: Routes attention over text-derived banks that can hold retrieved facts, a memory-retrieval use. No retrieval or tool-call decision is steered; the routing is attention-level.

title: First-Order Steering: Translating Weight Adaptation into Activation Steering
question: Can a differentiable model-merging procedure over LoRA adapters be turned into composable activation steering vectors, and which merges make those vectors accurate?
mechanism: For a merged model g(x, s) with steering strengths s, the first-order steering direction for behaviour i is a column of the Jacobian of the hidden layer with respect to s. Composed behaviours add as vectors. The approximation error is bounded by Hessian norms. HeRD-Merging trains per-subset matrices R_S by gradient descent to reduce the mixed-Jacobian and Hessian error terms while keeping merge accuracy.
training: yes: one LoRA adapter per target behaviour trained on steering directions, plus HeRD-Merging, which trains the matrices R_S by gradient descent (training-set size not captured)
setup: Qwen2.5-VL-3B, Gemma-4-E2B, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3; three target behaviours; baselines include CAA, RepE, ODESteer, Linear-AcT
numbers: HeRD-Merging achieves the highest overall behavioral adherence, at 79.9% (model-merging table, Table 3)
First-order steering: 42.5% on Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, and 32.0% on Gemma-4-E2B (Table 2 text); exceeds the best non-first-order baseline by 3.3 and 0.7 points
limits: Limitations section was not located in the extracted text. Evaluation covers three models and three behaviours. Authors note the composed-steering benefit of the trained terms is clearest on one model.
evidence_quote: Each column of the resulting Jacobian matrix defines a direction in activation space, and these directions can be naturally composed through vector addition.

novelty_note.E: The Hessian-norm error bound and the mixed-Jacobian terms for behaviour subsets measure how far composed steering departs from additivity (interference), before the vectors are used. The paper frames this as steering accuracy, not as patch interference.

title: Local Linearity of LLMs Enables Activation Steering via Model-Based Linear Optimal Control
question: Can steering be formulated as closed-loop LQR control over the layer-wise linearized dynamics of an LLM, so that the intervention tracks a feature setpoint without offline training?
mechanism: A-LQR: linearize each transformer block phi_k at the nominal trajectory (A_k = d phi_k / dz). Solve the finite-horizon LQR Riccati recursion for gains K_k and apply u_k = ubar_k - K_k dz_k at each layer. The feature setpoint beta_k* comes from a linear feature setpoint (LFS) procedure; the steering magnitude is adapted from the online-observed feature error v_k^T z_k - beta_k*. Error bounds are derived for tracking under linearization error (Thm. 4.2, Cor. 4.3).
training: none (training-free; Riccati gains computed from Jacobians)
inference_cost: gains computed in O(l d^3) time on CPU or O(log l * log^2 d) on GPU (Sec. 3.1, as stated); the Riccati recursion must be recomputed when the linearization changes (Sec. 3.1)
setup: Models and benchmarks not recovered: extracted text ends inside Sec. 4 (fulltext truncated before Sec. 5 experiments). Abstract mentions toxicity reduction, truthfulness, concept elicitation and jailbreaking across models and scales.
limits: Experimental results (Sec. 5) and the paper's own limitations were not available in the extracted full text, so no numbers are copied. Performance claims rest on the abstract. Linearization error is handled through bounds that assume closed-loop contraction.
evidence_quote: Applying LQR as in (5) for steering requires selecting an

novelty_note.B: The steering perturbation is scaled from the online-observed layer-wise feature error (a hidden-state feedback term), so it is state-dependent per layer. It is a feedback gain rather than a discrete gate, so this flag is partial.

title: When Does Activation Steering Change What a Model Computes From?
question: Does a successful activation steering vector recreate the state the model naturally uses, or only bias the output toward the target?
mechanism: Counterfactual register editing: estimate a rank-16 register subspace U from class-conditional mean differences at layer 12 (validation-selected). Edit z~ = z + Pi_U(mu(s~) - mu(s)) at the current-state token, flipping only the hidden bit. Score register agreement R and Counterfactual Update Selectivity CUS on discriminating items. Compare with mean-activation (function-vector-style) steering: transplant the target activation at one layer and scale the steering vector to the natural activation difference.
training: yes for the test models: fine-tuned 7B models (Qwen2.5-Coder-7B and a Llama 7B) to write running state (SFT, 11,346 training items per group); steering vectors themselves are not trained
setup: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B (main) and Llama 7B; Q8 and D8 state-tracking task (quaternion and dihedral groups)
numbers: Replacing the activation at one layer produces less than 2% of the target-answer margin gain from patching through all remaining layers (abstract)
Steering vectors have norms 77 and 26 times the median natural change in Qwen and Llama, producing 54% and 82% of the reference effect (abstract)
limits: Authors state the register experiments use explicit traces in controlled tasks, and the steering experiments test one effective task and layer per model with intervention at the final prompt token. The one-block patch tests restoration only at that site.
evidence_quote: U is the span of the leading r = 16 such directions at the validation-selected layer 12 edit site

novelty_note.G: Shows that steering vectors with norms 77 and 26 times the natural change still change the answer while failing to reproduce the natural target state, so the steering signal can reflect output biasing rather than the intended computed state.

title: HyperSteer: Activation Steering at Scale with Hypernetworks
question: Can one hypernetwork generate steering vectors for arbitrary steering prompts so steering scales to thousands of prompts and generalizes to unseen ones?
mechanism: A transformer hypernetwork H reads the steering prompt s. The cross-attention variant also reads the residual stream of the base LM on the base prompt x, and an MLP on the final token state outputs Delta_xs in R^d (Eqs. 2-3). Delta is added to the base model residual at layer 20. The hypernetwork is trained end-to-end with the LM cross-entropy of the steered output against AxBench labels (Eq. 4).
training: yes: end-to-end training of the hypernetwork on about 16,000 AxBench steering prompts (GemmaScope SAE labels), base:steering prompt ratio 72:1; hyperparameters in Table 3 (e.g. LR 8e-5, 3 epochs)
setup: Gemma-2-2B and Gemma-2-9B (instruction-tuned); AxBench Concept500 held-in and held-out; AlpacaEval base prompts; gpt-4o-mini judge
numbers: Cross Attention 0.608 0.742 0.934 1.091 (Table 1: Gemma-2-2b held-out, held-in, Gemma-2-9b held-out, held-in)
Prior best ReFT-r1 held-in 0.509 (2B) and 0.630 (9B) (Table 1)
limits: Authors state the approach falls slightly behind prompting and the best fine-tuning baselines on some measures. The concept datasets are limited in scope and quantity, which bounds quality and robustness. Steering vectors can be misused and should be audited.
evidence_quote: The hypernetwork outputs a steering vector that is added to the base LM residual stream.

novelty_note.D: A hypernetwork reads a natural-language steering prompt and outputs an activation modification, so a short instruction becomes a residual-stream intervention.

title: UniSteer: Text-Guided Flow Matching in Activation Space for Versatile LLM Steering
question: Can one text-conditioned flow over residual-stream activations replace a separate steering direction or module for each behaviour?
mechanism: Train a conditional flow model v_theta(a_t, t, c, l, i) over activations of a frozen LLM, with linear path a_t = (1-t) a_0 + t a_1, a_0 ~ N(0, I), target velocity a_1 - a_0, loss E||v_theta - u_t||^2 (Eqs. 2-4). Editing (flow inversion): partially invert the source activation under the source condition to tau = 1 - lambda, then transport forward under the target condition: a_edit = F_{tau->1}(F_{1->tau}(a_src; c_src); c_tgt). The edited activation is injected back into the frozen LLM. The same model classifies by reconstruction energy.
training: yes: conditional flow matching on activation-condition tuples from the frozen model (training-set size not captured)
inference_cost: ODE integration (forward and backward) per edited activation; number of steps and wall-clock not captured in extracted text
setup: Three target LLMs: Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen2.5-1.5B, Qwen2.5-7B; Persona, TruthfulQA Truth*Info, AxBench; baselines CAA, RepE, LoReFT, ODESteer
numbers: Table 1, UniSteer row (Persona / T*I / AxBench) for Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen2.5-1.5B and Qwen2.5-7B: 72.03 68.01 0.36 77.67 71.37 0.74 81.75 90.80 0.68
limits: Authors state the evaluations do not fully characterize effects on broader capabilities: long-form generation, multi-turn stability and complex reasoning were not evaluated.
evidence_quote: Solving the flow from 0 to 1 maps a prior sample to

novelty_note.D: The steering condition is a natural-language behaviour description (e.g. 'Be evil') that drives an activation transport, so text instructions become activation edits.

title: Self-Updatable Large Language Models by Integrating Context into Model Parameters
venue: ICLR 2025 (header states 'Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2025')
question: Can context be integrated into a model's parameters so the model answers questions about it without the context and without extra storage?
mechanism: SELF-PARAM: an original model with the context in its prompt is the teacher. The target model is the same network without the context. Minimize KL divergence between the teacher's and target's next-token predictions over a target sentence set (generated QA pairs from an instruct model plus sentences from the pretraining data). No new parameters are added and no retrieval is used at inference.
training: yes: gradient updates of the target model's parameters on the target sentence set (size not captured in extraction)
inference_cost: zero additional parameters or storage, per the abstract
setup: Mistral-7B and Llama3-8B; single and batch context injection (100 and 500 contexts); sequential injection; conversational recommendation
numbers: Table 4 (target-sentence-set model ablation), columns Mistral-7B and Llama3-8B at 100 contexts, then Mistral-7B and Llama3-8B at 500 contexts: 4o-mini 0.4521 0.4368 0.4384 0.4221; instruct 0.4502 0.4341 0.4836 0.4464
limits: No limitations section was located in the extracted text. Fine-tuning on the raw contexts or on the target sentence set (FT(C), FT(S)) is reported to fall well short, which the authors attribute to style divergence.
evidence_quote: Our method employs a training objective that minimizes the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between the predictions of an original model (with access to contextual information) and a target model (without such access).

novelty_note.D: Distils an instruction or context into weights by matching the output distribution with and without the context, so context becomes a weight modification.

title: Belief Dynamics Reveal the Dual Nature of In-Context Learning and Activation Steering
question: Do ICL and activation steering both act by updating belief in latent concepts, and can a closed-form model predict their effect?
mechanism: Bayesian account: log posterior odds of concept c given context x are log(p(c)/p(c')) + evidence from the context + a*m, where m is steering magnitude (Sec. 4.3). The prior-odds term is replaced by a constant offset b. ICL evidence accumulates with context length N and with the number of shots, giving a sigmoidal behaviour curve; steering gives a sigmoidal trend in the magnitude. Parameters a, b, gamma, alpha are fitted to averaged behaviour by L-BFGS.
training: none for the model itself; a few scalar parameters are fitted to averaged behaviour with L-BFGS
setup: Llama-3.1-8B (persona-matching: Dark Triad and Moral Nihilism datasets; flipped-label sentiment); Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct analysis
numbers: Tested steering magnitude range: m in [-3, 3] for the Dark Triad datasets, [-1.5, 1.5] for Moral Nihilism (Llama-3.1-8B; Sec. 4.2 text, a tested range rather than a result)
limits: Steering vectors used in practice are not the true concept vectors, so the magnitude-to-effect scale is only proportional. The prior odds b are estimated rather than observed from the concept priors p(c). The model is a predictive account on the tested tasks and contexts.
evidence_quote: since it does not depend on the precise input x or its representation v

novelty_note.E: Predicts the context length or steering magnitude at which the behaviour flips, from a closed-form fit, and states that ICL and steering interventions are additive in log-belief space, which would predict the combined effect of two interventions.
